title: Problems: stops, costs, false alarms and the years of evidence

items.prose: A desk trades the spread $y - 1.15x$ of two glassmakers' shares, with $y$ at £48.00 and $x$ at £36.00. A share sold short must be borrowed, and the lender charges a fee on the pounds borrowed. It is 0.5% a year for $y$, but 6% a year for $x$, which few lenders hold. Take a year as 252 trading days and the prices as fixed while a trade is open. Every trade is held for 21 trading days, and one unit of $z$ is worth £0.50 of spread.

parts.question: When the desk is long the spread, how many pounds of stock does it borrow? Give your answer in pounds to 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: A long buys one $y$ and sells 1.15 shares of $x$, so it borrows $1.15 \times £36.00 = £41.40$ of $x$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out which share a long spread sells, then price that leg.

byKey.y-leg: £48.00 is the $y$ leg, which a long buys. The borrowed leg is the one it sells, 1.15 shares of $x$.
byKey.no-hedge: £36.00 is one share of $x$. A long sells 1.15 of them for each $y$.
byKey.hedge-on-y: You multiplied $y$'s price by 1.15. The ratio counts shares of $x$, at £36.00 each.

explain.text: Long the spread is long $y$ and short $1.15x$. Only the short leg is borrowed, and it is worth $1.15 \times 36.00 = £41.40$.

parts.question: Using £41.40, what does a long trade pay in borrowing fees over its 21 days? Give pounds to 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: 21 days is $21/252 = 1/12$ of a year, so the fee is $41.40 \times 0.06/12 = £0.207$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Charge 6% a year on £41.40 for 21 of the year's 252 trading days.

byKey.calendar-days: You divided by 365. The fee here runs on 252 trading days, so 21 days is $1/12$ of a year.
byKey.one-day: That is one day's fee, $2.484/252$. The trade is held for 21 days.
byKey.annual: £2.484 is a whole year's fee. The trade lasts 21 of the 252 days.
byKey.y-rate: You charged $y$'s 0.5%. A long borrows $x$, whose fee is 6%.

explain.text: A year's fee on £41.40 at 6% is £2.484. The trade lasts $21/252 = 1/12$ of a year, so it pays £0.207.

parts.question: Using £0.207, how much more does a 21-day long pay in fees than a 21-day short? Give pounds to 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: A short borrows one $y$: $48.00 \times 0.005/12 = £0.020$. The long pays $0.207 - 0.020 = £0.187$ more.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Price a short's fee on the leg it sells, for 21 days, then subtract it from £0.207.

byKey.short-only: £0.020 is the short's own fee. The question asks how much more the long pays.
byKey.sum: You added the two fees. The question asks for the gap between them, $0.207 - 0.020$.
byKey.x-rate-both: You charged the short at 6%. It borrows $y$, whose fee is 0.5% a year.

explain.text: A short sells $y$, so it borrows £48.00 of $y$ at 0.5% a year: £0.020 over 21 days. The cheap borrow on $y$ leaves the long £0.187 worse off per trade.

parts.question: A backtest of the rule with entry ±2 and exit 0 leaves out borrowing fees. What does that do to its results?

options.text: It overstates each long by £0.207 and each short by £0.020, so it flatters the longs most
Nothing, since a spread trade is hedged and the fees cancel across the legs
options.why: Only the sold leg is borrowed, so nothing cancels. Each trade pays on one leg.

options.text: Only the shorts look better, since shorting the spread is the side that sells
options.why: Both sides sell a share. A short spread sells $y$ and a long sells $1.15x$.

options.text: It understates the results, since lending the shares earns the desk interest
options.why: The desk is the borrower, so it pays the fee. Leaving it out makes every trade look better.

feedback.correct: Correct. Each trade misses the fee on its sold leg, and the long's is over ten times the short's.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask which leg each side sells, and what borrowing it costs over 21 days.

byKey.no-effect: Only the sold leg is borrowed, so nothing cancels. Each trade pays on one leg.
byKey.short-only: Both sides sell a share. A short spread sells $y$ and a long sells $1.15x$.
byKey.understates: The desk is the borrower, so it pays the fee. Leaving it out makes every trade look better.

explain.text: Each side sells one leg and borrows it: the long $x$ at £0.207 a trade, the short $y$ at £0.020. A backtest without the fees overstates both, the longs by far the more.

parts.question: A short opened at $z = 2$ and closed at 0 nets $2 \times 0.50 - 0.020 = £0.98$ after fees. Using £0.187, where must a long open, closing at 0, to net the same? Give the $z$ level to 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The long needs $0.187/0.50 = 0.374$ more units of $z$, so it opens at $-2 - 0.374 = -2.37$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn the extra £0.187 into units of $z$ at £0.50 each, then move the long entry out by that much.

byKey.sign: A long opens below the mean, so its entry is negative: −2.37.
byKey.shift-only: 0.37 is how far the entry moves. The entry itself is $-2 - 0.374 = -2.37$.
byKey.pounds: You added £0.187 to a $z$ level. Divide by £0.50 first: 0.374 units of $z$.
byKey.wrong-way: −1.63 moves the entry towards the mean, which earns less. The long needs more room, so its entry moves out.

explain.text: From −2.37 to 0 a long earns $2.374 \times 0.50 = £1.187$, and its fees take £0.207, leaving £0.98. A desk that ignores borrowing fees opens its longs too early.

items.prose: A spread is traded on its z-score with entry at 2, exit at 0 and stop at 3.4. A short opens at exactly $z = 2$. One unit of $z$ is worth £0.60 per unit of the pair, and a round trip costs £0.10. Assume each trade ends exactly at the exit or exactly at the stop.

parts.question: What does a trade that reaches the exit earn, net of costs, in pounds? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $z$ falls 2 units, worth $2 \times 0.60 = £1.20$; less £0.10 of costs, £1.10.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn the 2 units of $z$ into pounds, then take off the costs.

byKey.no-cost: That is before costs. Take off the £0.10 round trip.
byKey.cost-added: You added the cost. It is paid, so subtract it.
byKey.z-units: You subtracted the cost from 2 units of $z$. Turn $z$ into pounds first: $2 \times 0.60$.

explain.text: From entry at 2 to exit at 0 the short gains 2 units of $z$, £1.20. The round trip costs £0.10, which leaves £1.10.

parts.question: What does a trade that hits the stop earn, net of costs, in pounds? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $z$ rises 1.4 units against the short, $1.4 \times 0.60 = £0.84$; with £0.10 of costs, $-£0.94$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The stop is 1.4 units above the entry. Turn that into pounds and add the cost to the loss.

byKey.no-cost: That is before costs. The round trip adds £0.10 to the loss.
byKey.stop-four: You used a stop at 4. Here the stop is at 3.4, only 1.4 units above the entry.
byKey.sign: A stopped short has lost: the spread ran 1.4 units the wrong way.
byKey.cost-wrong-way: You took the cost off the loss. Costs make a loss bigger.

explain.text: The stop is $3.4 - 2 = 1.4$ units above the entry, a loss of $1.4 \times 0.60 = £0.84$. With the round trip's £0.10, a stopped trade loses £0.94.

parts.question: Using £1.10 and $-£0.94$, what share of trades must reach the exit for the rule to break even? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Set $1.10p - 0.94(1 - p) = 0$ and solve for $p$.

byKey.swapped: That is $1.10/2.04$. The share reaching the exit is the loss over the sum: $0.94/2.04$.
byKey.no-cost: That uses the pounds before costs, $0.84/2.04$. Use the net figures, £1.10 and £0.94.
byKey.even: Half would suit a gain and a loss of equal size. Here the gain is the larger, so a little under half will do.

explain.text: An exit earns £1.10 and a stop loses £0.94, so $1.10p = 0.94(1 - p)$. That gives $p = 0.94/2.04 = 0.461$: the rule pays if more than 46.1% of trades reach the exit.

parts.question: If the pair has broken, $z$ wanders like a driftless walk. Started between two levels, such a walk reaches the lower one first with chance $d_{\text{up}}/(d_{\text{up}} + d_{\text{down}})$. Here $d$ is the distance to each level. What is the chance the short reaches the exit first? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The stop is 1.4 away and the levels are 3.4 apart: $1.4/3.4 = 0.412$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The upper level is the stop at 3.4 and the lower is the exit at 0.

byKey.swapped: That is $2/3.4$, the chance of reaching the stop first. The exit's chance is $1.4/3.4$.
byKey.even: The two levels are not the same distance away. The stop is nearer, so it comes first more often.

explain.text: From $z = 2$ the stop is 1.4 units up and the exit 2 units down. A fair walk reaches the nearer level more often, so the exit comes first only $1.4/3.4 = 0.412$ of the time.

parts.question: Using 0.412 for the broken pair, with £1.10 and $-£0.94$, what is the expected net P&L per trade, in pounds? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $0.412 \times 1.10 - 0.588 \times 0.94 = -£0.10$, the cost of a round trip.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Weight the exit's £1.10 by 0.412 and the stop's $-£0.94$ by $1 - 0.412$.

byKey.no-cost: That is before costs: $0.412 \times 1.20 - 0.588 \times 0.84 = 0$. The net figures give −£0.10.
byKey.sign: The broken pair falls short of the 0.461 needed to break even, so it loses on average.
byKey.even: You used even odds. On the broken pair the exit comes first with chance 0.412.

explain.text: Before costs the bet is fair: $0.412 \times 1.20 - 0.588 \times 0.84 = 0$. So a broken pair loses the £0.10 of costs on each trade, whatever the thresholds; the stop sets only the size of each loss.

items.prose: A fund trades 43 pairs and checks each spread's rolling half-life once a month. A check breaches when the half-life passes the fund's limit. A healthy pair breaches with chance 0.14 at each check, independently, and a broken pair breaches at every check. Suppose 3 pairs break before the first check and the other 40 stay healthy. Rule A stops a pair at its first breach; rule B waits for two breaches in a row.

parts.question: What is the chance that rule A stops a given healthy pair within the first four checks? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: A healthy pair passes all four checks with chance $0.86^4 = 0.5470$, so rule A stops it with chance $1 - 0.5470 = 0.4530$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the chance that all four checks pass, then take it from 1.

byKey.added: You added 0.14 four times. That counts a pair with two breaches twice; use $1 - 0.86^4$.
byKey.escape: That is the chance of four clean checks. Rule A stops the pair in every other case.
byKey.all-four: That is the chance that all four checks breach. One breach is enough for rule A.

explain.text: Rule A misses a healthy pair only if all four checks pass, which has chance $0.86^4 = 0.5470$. Every other run of checks holds a breach, so the chance is 0.4530.

parts.question: What is the chance that rule B stops a given healthy pair within the first four checks? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The first double breach is at checks 1 and 2, 2 and 3, or 3 and 4. The later two need a pass just before. So the chance is $0.14^2(1 + 0.86 + 0.86) = 0.0533$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Split by the first pair of neighbouring checks that both breach; those cases cannot overlap.

byKey.three-pairs: You added $0.14^2$ three times. A later pair of checks counts only after a pass at the check before it.
byKey.one-pair: That is one given pair of checks, $0.14^2$. Rule B can fire at check 2, 3 or 4.
byKey.overlap: You treated the three pairs of checks as independent, but neighbouring pairs share a check.

explain.text: Two given checks both breach with chance $0.14^2 = 0.0196$. A double breach at checks 2 and 3, or 3 and 4, also needs a pass just before it. So the chance is $0.0196 \times (1 + 0.86 + 0.86) = 0.0196 \times 2.72 = 0.0533$.

parts.question: Over four checks, how many more of the 40 healthy pairs should rule A stop than rule B? Use 0.4530 and 0.0533, and give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Rule A stops $40 \times 0.4530 = 18.12$ healthy pairs and rule B $40 \times 0.0533 = 2.13$: 15.99 more.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply each chance by the 40 healthy pairs, then subtract.

byKey.a-only: That is rule A's own count. The question asks how many more than rule B's 2.13.
byKey.all-43: You counted all 43 pairs. Both rules stop the 3 broken pairs, and those stops are not false ones.
byKey.b-only: That is rule B's count. Rule A stops far more: 18.12.

explain.text: Each rule's expected number of false stops is 40 times its chance. That gives 18.12 for rule A and 2.13 for rule B, a gap of 15.99 healthy pairs.

parts.question: On a broken pair, rule A stops at check 1 and rule B at check 2. Each month of delay on a broken pair costs £5.00, and each false stop gives up £1.75. Using 15.99, by how many pounds is rule B cheaper over the four checks? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Rule B avoids $15.99 \times 1.75 = £27.98$ of false stops and pays $3 \times 5.00 = £15.00$ of delay: it is £12.98 cheaper.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Price the false stops rule B avoids, then take off the delay it costs on the 3 broken pairs.

byKey.no-delay: That is the saving on false stops alone. Rule B also waits one more month on each of the 3 broken pairs.
byKey.one-broken: You charged the delay on one broken pair. All 3 wait a month longer under rule B.
byKey.sign: Rule B saves more on false stops than it loses in delay, so it is the cheaper rule.

explain.text: Rule B avoids 15.99 false stops at £1.75 each, £27.98 in all. It stops each of the 3 broken pairs a month later, at £5.00 each. So it is cheaper by $27.98 - 15.00 = £12.98$.

parts.question: Rule B saves £27.98 on false stops. At what cost per month of delay would the two rules cost the same? Give your answer in pounds to 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The rules match when $3c = 27.98$, so $c = £9.33$ a month.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Set the delay cost on the 3 broken pairs equal to the £27.98 saved on false stops.

byKey.no-split: That is the whole saving. It is set against 3 broken pairs' delay, so divide by 3.
byKey.margin: You divided the £12.98 margin by 3. That is how far the cost could rise, so add it to £5.00: £9.33.

explain.text: Rule B's saving on false stops stays at £27.98, while its delay costs 3 months at $c$ each. They match at $c = 27.98/3 = £9.33$. Below that, waiting for a second breach is the cheaper rule.

items.prose: Two housebuilders' shares were chosen as a pair and fitted on four years of daily closes, then traded on the next 504 days. Those trading days earned £18.90 per unit of the pair after costs, and the daily P&L had sd £0.55. Take a Sharpe ratio over $T$ years to have a standard error of about $1/\sqrt T$.

parts.question: What was the mean daily P&L over the trading days, in pounds? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the £18.90 by the 504 trading days.

byKey.all-days: You divided by all 1,512 days. The four fitting years are not part of the test; only the 504 trading days are.
byKey.per-252: You divided by 252, one year. The trading ran for 504 days, two years.

explain.text: Only the trading days earned the £18.90, so the mean is taken over 504 days: $18.90/504 = £0.0375$. The four fitting years chose the pair and play no part in judging it.

parts.question: Using a mean of £0.0375 and an sd of £0.55, what is the annualised Sharpe ratio? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the daily mean by the daily sd, then multiply by $\sqrt{252}$.

byKey.daily: That is the daily ratio. Multiply by $\sqrt{252} = 15.87$ to annualise it.
byKey.times-252: You multiplied by 252. The sd grows like the root of time, so annualise with $\sqrt{252}$.
byKey.variance: You divided by the variance, 0.3025. The Sharpe ratio divides by the sd, £0.55.

explain.text: The daily ratio is $0.0375/0.55 = 0.0682$. Over a year the mean adds up 252 times while the sd grows by $\sqrt{252}$. So the annual figure is $0.0682 \times 15.87 = 1.08$.

parts.question: The Sharpe of 1.08 was earned over the 504 trading days. Divide it by its standard error. What do you get? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Two years of trading give a standard error of $1/\sqrt 2 = 0.707$, and $1.08/0.707 = 1.53$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn the 504 days into years, find $1/\sqrt T$, then divide 1.08 by it.

byKey.times-t: Doubling gives 2.16, which treats the standard error as $\tfrac12$. With $T = 2$ it is $1/\sqrt 2 = 0.707$.
byKey.divided: 0.76 is $1.08 \times 0.707$. The standard error goes underneath: $1.08/0.707$.
byKey.all-years: Six years would give 2.65, but four of them only fitted the pair. The Sharpe was earned on two.

explain.text: $504/252 = 2$, so $T = 2$ and the standard error is about 0.707. The ratio $1.08/0.707 = 1.53$ falls short of the usual mark of 2, so two years have not yet settled the matter.

parts.question: If the Sharpe stays at 1.08, how many years of trading would lift that ratio to 2? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $1.08\sqrt T = 2$ gives $\sqrt T = 1.852$, so $T = 3.43$ years.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Set $1.08\sqrt T = 2$ and solve for $T$.

byKey.no-square: That is $\sqrt T$. Square it: $1.852^2 = 3.43$ years.
byKey.inverted: You squared $1.08/2$. The equation $1.08\sqrt T = 2$ gives $\sqrt T = 2/1.08$.
byKey.four-over: You squared the 2 but not the 1.08. $T = 2^2/1.08^2 = 4/1.1664$.

explain.text: A Sharpe of $S$ over $T$ years sits $S\sqrt T$ standard errors from zero. Setting $1.08\sqrt T = 2$ gives $T = (2/1.08)^2 = 3.43$ years.

parts.question: A year has 252 trading days. Using 3.43 years, how many days does the desk need beyond the 504 it has? Round up to a whole number of days.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn 3.43 years into days, then take off the 504 already traded.

byKey.total: That is the whole span, 864.4 days rounded up. The desk already has 504 of them.
byKey.round-down: After 360 more days the total is still short of 864.4. Round up to 361.

explain.text: 3.43 years is $3.43 \times 252 = 864.4$ trading days. The desk has 504, so it needs 360.4 more, which is 361 whole days. If the Sharpe holds, that is well over another year before it clears 2 standard errors.
